555-timer-calculator/can-i-get-a-50-perc.text:
Can I get a 50% duty cycle from a 555 timer?

Not from the standard two-resistor astable — but a single diode fixes it, and opens up any duty cycle, not just 50%. Put your target frequency and duty cycle in and get the resistors to buy. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

← 555 timer calculator · All free electronics tools

Design the diode-mod astable

Pick the capacitor you have, the frequency and duty cycle you want — any value from just above 0% to just below 100% — and get the exact R1/R2, the nearest standard (E24) values, and what those buyable resistors really produce.

Common questions

Can I get a 50% duty cycle from a 555 timer?

Not from the standard two-resistor astable — it charges through R1 + R2 and discharges through R2 alone, so the high time is always longer than the low time and 50% is a limit it only approaches, never reaches. Add a diode across R2, forward-biased so it shorts R2 out of the charge path, and the capacitor charges through R1 alone instead. High time and low time no longer share a resistor, so any duty cycle is possible, including 50% or below.

What resistor values give an exact 50% duty cycle with the diode mod?

R1 = R2. With the diode in place, high time is ln(2) times R1 times C and low time is ln(2) times R2 times C, so they are equal exactly when the resistors are equal — and the frequency formula collapses to the familiar single-resistor form, f = 1 divided by (2 times ln(2) times R times C).

Does the diode need to be a specific type?

Any small switching diode works electrically — a 1N4148 is the usual choice. What varies is its forward voltage drop while conducting: roughly 0.6 to 0.7 V for silicon, lower for a Schottky part. That drop is not in the formula below, so it is a real source of error, worse at low supply voltages or a small R1 where the drop is a bigger fraction of the charging voltage. A Schottky diode shrinks that error; it does not change which duty cycles are reachable.

Can the diode mod reach duty cycles below 50%, not just down to it?

Yes. Duty cycle is R1 divided by (R1 + R2) once the diode is in place, and that ratio is free to land anywhere between 0% and 100% by choosing R1 smaller or larger than R2 — the 50%-or-above restriction was specific to the plain two-resistor astable, and the diode removes it rather than just extending it to exactly 50%.

555-timer-calculator/index.html.text:
555 Timer Calculator

Astable (oscillator) and monostable (one-shot), in both directions: analyse the parts you have, or design from the frequency, duty cycle, or pulse width you want down to resistors you can actually buy. Everything runs in this page — nothing is uploaded.

← All free electronics tools

Astable — what do my parts do?

The standard two-resistor oscillator. The capacitor charges through R1 + R2 and discharges through R2 alone.

Astable — design for a target

Pick the capacitor you have, say what frequency and duty cycle you want, and get the exact R1/R2 plus the nearest standard (E24) values — and what those buyable resistors really produce.

Must be above 50 — see below. Need 50% or less? Use the diode-mod calculator.

Monostable — one-shot pulse

A trigger starts a single output pulse of ln(3) × R × C (the familiar 1.1 RC), after which the output falls regardless of the input.

Design for a target pulse width

Why the numbers and the bench disagree

The timing equations have no opinion about whether a design is buildable, which is where most 555 projects actually go wrong:

  • A standard astable can't do 50% duty or below. Charging goes through R1 + R2, discharging through R2 alone, so high time always exceeds low time. It approaches 50% as R2 grows relative to R1 and never reaches it. A diode across R2 (so charging bypasses R2) buys you 50% and below.
  • R1 sets the discharge current. When discharge begins, R1 alone limits current into the discharge pin, which sinks roughly 200 mA at most. This page checks that against your supply voltage.
  • Big timing resistors drift. Past about 1 MΩ the threshold pin's own leakage stops being negligible next to the charging current on a bipolar NE555, so the real period wanders — with temperature, and between chips. A CMOS 555 (7555/TLC555) is far more tolerant.
  • Electrolytic timing caps are approximate. −20%/+80% is a common tolerance, so a microfarad-scale design's frequency is a target, not a specification. Trim with R2 if it matters.

Common questions

Why can't a 555 astable produce a 50% duty cycle?

In the standard two-resistor astable the timing capacitor charges through R1 + R2 but discharges through R2 alone, so the output-high time is always longer than the output-low time. The duty cycle approaches 50% as R2 grows relative to R1 but never reaches it. To get 50% or below, put a diode across R2 so charging bypasses it, or use a CMOS 555 in a 50%-duty configuration.

What is the 555 astable frequency formula?

The period is ln(2) × (R1 + 2 × R2) × C, which is where the familiar f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 × R2) × C) comes from — 1.44 is 1 / ln(2). The output-high time is ln(2) × (R1 + R2) × C and the output-low time is ln(2) × R2 × C.

How long is a 555 monostable pulse?

ln(3) × R × C, usually quoted as the rule of thumb 1.1 × R × C. The capacitor charges from 0 V to the 2/3 Vcc threshold, and ln(3) is the time constant multiple that takes.

How small can R1 be in a 555 astable?

About 1 kΩ in practice. During the discharge phase R1 is the only thing limiting current into the 555's discharge pin, which sinks at most around 200 mA. A smaller R1 satisfies the timing equations but can exceed that rating.

Free electronics calculators

Small, sharp tools for the parts of circuit design that are easy to get subtly wrong. Every one is free with no signup, runs entirely in your browser, and never uploads what you type — there is no server for it to go to.

  • Resistor color code & Ohm's law calculator

    Decode a 4-band or 5-band resistor into its resistance and tolerance, and solve Ohm's law and power — give it any two of V, I, R, and P and it fills in the rest.

    "What is brown-black-red-gold?" → 1 kΩ ±5%.

  • LED series resistor calculator

    Size the current-limiting resistor for one or several LEDs in series, snap it to a resistor you can actually buy (E24), and check the power rating you need so the resistor doesn't run hot.

    "Red LED, 5V supply, 20mA?" → 150 Ω dissipating 60 mW, so a ⅛W part is enough.

    Several LEDs? Series, one resistor each, or one shared?

  • Voltage divider calculator

    Compute a divider's output including the sag a real load causes — the loading correction the textbook formula ignores — or design a divider for a target output voltage using a buyable E24 resistor.

    "12V, two 10k resistors, 1k load?" → not 6V, and the tool shows how far off.

  • 555 timer calculator

    Astable and monostable, in both directions: analyse the parts you have, or design from a target frequency, duty cycle, or pulse width. Flags the designs a real chip can't run — duty cycles at or below 50%, an R1 that over-currents the discharge pin, drift-prone resistor values.

    "1 kHz at 60% duty from a 100nF cap?" → the exact R1/R2 and the E24 pair to buy.

  • RC / RL filter calculator

    Cutoff frequency and time constant for all four first-order topologies (RC or RL, low-pass or high-pass), plus a design mode that solves for the missing component from a target cutoff and snaps it to a value you can actually buy.

    "1 kHz low-pass with a 100nF cap?" → 1.59 kΩ, nearest E24 1.6 kΩ.

  • RC charge and discharge time calculator

    Find the time to reach a real capacitor voltage threshold, or design a buyable resistor or capacitor for a target delay.

    "How long to charge 100 nF through 10 kΩ to 3.16 V from 5 V?" → about 1 ms.

    No threshold in mind yet? How long until it's basically fully charged?

Common questions

Why did the voltage divider calculator give a different answer than Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2)?

Because that textbook formula assumes nothing is drawing current from the output. Add a real load and the divider sags — the calculator's loading correction accounts for the load resistor pulling R2 down, which is why “12V, two 10k resistors, 1k load” does not come out to 6V.

Are the resistor and capacitor values these tools suggest ones I can actually buy?

Where a tool has a design mode — the LED, voltage-divider, 555-timer, RC-filter, and RC-time calculators — it snaps the computed value to the nearest standard E24 part and shows you the exact pair, instead of leaving you to source an odd value like 8,342 Ω.

Can I use these for a safety-critical or production design?

No. They are educational calculators for getting the arithmetic right, not a substitute for reading a datasheet, checking a component's real tolerances, or measuring the circuit you actually built. Treat any output as a starting point to verify, especially anything touching mains voltage or driving real current.

How is this different from a general calculator site like Omni Calculator?

See the full comparison — in short, a general calculator site answers one formula among thousands of unrelated topics, while these six tools snap a design to a resistor or capacitor you can actually buy and flag a 555 design a real chip can't run.

Could I just work these formulas out by hand instead?

Yes — see the full comparison. Every formula here is a standard, published equation; what these tools add is snapping the answer to a resistor or capacitor you can actually buy and flagging a 555 design a real chip can't run, both easy steps to skip when working a formula out on paper.

Does anything I type get uploaded anywhere?

No — there is no server for it to go to. Every calculation runs in your browser, and the only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features get used, kept in your own browser's storage and easy to turn off on each tool's page.

led-resistor-calculator/can-i-use-one-re.text:
Can I use one resistor for multiple LEDs?

Yes — if they are in series. Sharing one resistor across LEDs wired in parallel is the version that quietly kills LEDs, and it does not even save power. Put your numbers in and compare all three wirings. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

← LED series resistor calculator · All free electronics tools

Your supply and LEDs

From the LED's datasheet. 20 mA is common for 5 mm indicator LEDs; many are rated lower.

Common questions

Can I use one resistor for multiple LEDs?

Yes, if the LEDs are in series — and that is the good version. In a series string there is only one current, so one resistor sets it for every LED. On this page's defaults (9 V supply, 2.0 V LEDs at 20 mA, four LEDs) that is a single 50 Ω resistor, or 51 Ω as the nearest part you can actually buy.

Sharing one resistor across LEDs wired in parallel also lights them, but the resistor then fixes only the total current. How that total divides between the LEDs is set by their forward-voltage curves, which the resistor cannot influence — every LED sits across the same node.

Does a shared resistor save power compared with one resistor per LED?

No. It saves parts, not power, which surprises most people the first time. Both parallel wirings drop the same voltage (supply minus one forward voltage) at the same total current, so they waste identically: on the defaults, 0.72 W drawn from the supply, 0.16 W of it doing useful work in the LEDs and 0.56 W leaving as heat either way.

What changes is where the heat goes. Four separate 350 Ω resistors dissipate 0.14 W each and want 0.5 W parts. The single shared 87.5 Ω resistor takes all 0.56 W by itself and wants a 2 W part — a much bigger component than most people reach for when they are trying to save one.

What actually goes wrong with one shared resistor?

The current divides by forward voltage rather than evenly. LEDs off the same reel differ slightly; the one with the lowest forward voltage takes more than its share, heats up, drops further, and takes more still.

The split is not predictable without each LED's own measured curve, so this page does not pretend to predict it. The bound is certain: the resistor holds the total, so if one LED ends up carrying that total alone, it carries all of it. Four LEDs designed for 20 mA each give a ceiling of 80 mA through a single 20 mA part.

How many LEDs can I put in one series string?

As many as fit inside the supply voltage with something left over for the resistor. A string that consumed the whole supply would leave the resistor 0 V, and then nothing sets the current at all. On a 9 V supply with 2.0 V LEDs that is four — 8 V of LEDs and 1 V for the resistor. A fifth would need 10 V.

Where the string does not fit, give each LED its own resistor. That wiring is always available, because each branch only ever needs one forward voltage of headroom no matter how many branches there are.

Why does a series string waste so much less power?

Because the supply delivers the design current once instead of once per LED. Four LEDs in series draw 20 mA in total on the defaults; four parallel branches draw 80 mA for the same light, and the extra ends up in the resistors as heat — 0.02 W wasted by the string against 0.56 W by four separate resistors, or 89% efficient against 22%. On a battery that is the difference between hours and a fraction of one.

led-resistor-calculator/index.html.text:
LED Series Resistor Calculator

Figure out the current-limiting resistor for an LED (or a string of LEDs in series) before you burn one out. Everything runs in this page — nothing is uploaded.

← All free electronics tools

Circuit values

Check the LED's datasheet — 20 mA is a common default for 5 mm indicator LEDs, but many are rated lower.

Lighting more than one LED? Compare a series string, one resistor each, and one shared resistor — including why a shared resistor across parallel LEDs saves parts but not power.

Common questions

What resistor does this page's own default (9 V supply, one 2 V LED at 20 mA) need?

Exactly 350 Ω, dissipating 0.14 W. The nearest standard (E24) resistor is 360 Ω, which runs the LED at 19.44 mA instead of 20 mA and dissipates 0.136 W. This calculator recommends a 0.5 W part for it — it doubles the dissipation for a safety margin before picking a standard wattage, and 2× 0.14 W = 0.28 W crosses the 0.25 W step, so it rounds up to 0.5 W.

How does adding more LEDs in series change the resistor?

Each LED's forward voltage subtracts from the headroom the resistor has to work with. Put three of this page's default 2 V LEDs in series (6 V total) on the same 9 V supply and the exact resistor drops to 150 Ω, dissipating 60 mW — and 150 Ω is itself a standard E24 value, so the nearest-standard row matches it exactly and the LEDs run at the full 20 mA target.

Why does the calculator refuse some inputs instead of showing a result?

Because the supply voltage has to exceed the LEDs' total forward voltage with headroom left over for the resistor — without that headroom there is no valid resistor value. Five of this page's default 2 V LEDs in series need 10 V total, which exceeds the 9 V default supply, so the calculator reports the shortfall rather than returning a negative or zero resistance.

rc-filter-calculator/index.html.text:
RC / RL Filter Cutoff Frequency Calculator

Find the −3 dB cutoff frequency and time constant of a first-order RC or RL filter — or work backwards from a target cutoff to the component you need. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

← All free electronics tools

Filter

What do you want to do?

The solved component is snapped to the nearest standard preferred value you can actually buy, and the cutoff that value really produces is shown.

Common questions

How do I calculate the cutoff frequency of an RC filter?

For a first-order RC filter the -3 dB cutoff frequency is f_c = 1 / (2·π·R·C), where R is in ohms and C is in farads. The time constant is τ = R·C. Whether the filter is low-pass or high-pass only changes where the output is taken, not the cutoff frequency.

What is the cutoff frequency of an RL filter?

For a first-order RL filter the -3 dB cutoff frequency is f_c = R / (2·π·L), with R in ohms and L in henries. The time constant is τ = L / R.

What does the -3 dB cutoff frequency mean?

It is the frequency at which the filter's output power has fallen to half of the input (voltage down to about 70.7%). Beyond it, a first-order filter rolls off at -20 dB per decade (-6 dB per octave).

What this is (and isn't)

This covers the standard first-order (single R with a single C or L) passive filter. It reports the −3 dB cutoff frequency, the angular cutoff, and the time constant. It does not model higher-order filters, component tolerances, source/load impedance loading, parasitics, or the full frequency response — treat the numbers as the ideal textbook design point, then verify against your real parts and datasheets.

rc-filter-calculator/vs-picking-a-compon.text:
This calculator vs. picking a resistor or capacitor from the parts bin

Grabbing a component that's "about right" is fast, and it's how most prototype filters get built. The part missing from that habit isn't knowledge of the formula -- it's the second calculation nobody does: what cutoff does the part you actually grabbed produce, and how far is that from the one you designed for?

← RC / RL filter cutoff calculator · All free electronics tools

What each approach actually answers

Picking a component from the bin answers "do I have something in roughly the right range?" -- a quick, reasonable first question. What it doesn't answer is the one that decides whether the filter does what you designed it for: the exact value a target cutoff needs is almost never a value that gets sold, so any real build already involves rounding, and rounding by eye means the size of that rounding error is simply unknown until someone sits down with the formula and the actual part.

This calculator does that second step for you. Give it a target cutoff and one known component, and its design mode solves for the exact value the other component needs, snaps it to the nearest value in the standard series you'd actually buy (E12 for capacitors and inductors, E24 for resistors), and reports the cutoff and signed error percent that snapped value really produces -- so "close enough" is a number you read off the page rather than a guess you carry into the build.

Neither replaces the other. You still choose the part; the tool just tells you, before you solder it in, exactly what cutoff that choice gives you.

Where a bin-picked value typically goes wrong

HabitWhat it does to the real cutoff
Grabbing a value from the wrong decadeA 10 nF part picked up in place of a 100 nF one shifts the cutoff by a factor of 10 -- easy to do by eye when two reels or drawers are labelled similarly.
Assuming a value is in the standard seriesPreferred-value resistors step in the E24 series and most stocked capacitors in E12; a value that looks plausible can simply not exist as a part, forcing a substitution nobody planned for.
Never recomputing after the substitutionThe single most common gap: a part is swapped in because it's close, and the cutoff it actually produces is never worked back out, so the error is unknown rather than small.
Ignoring the part's own toleranceA real resistor or capacitor carries its own ±5% to ±20% tolerance on top of whatever rounding error the substitution already introduced -- two separate sources of drift that stack rather than cancel.

This calculator can't stock your parts bin for you -- it can only compute correctly once you tell it which component you actually have or picked. What it removes is redoing the cutoff-frequency arithmetic by hand after that choice.

Common questions

Isn't grabbing a close resistor or capacitor good enough for most filters?

Sometimes -- if the application has generous margin, close is fine. The risk is that "close" is a guess about the component value, not about the cutoff frequency it produces, and those two aren't the same distance apart. A resistor or capacitor picked because it's "about right" from a mixed parts bin can land the real -3 dB cutoff anywhere from a few percent off to a full octave or more away from the one the design actually called for, with nothing about the build itself signaling the mismatch.

What actually goes wrong when you round a component value in your head?

Three separate mistakes tend to compound: reaching for a value from the wrong decade (10 nF picked up instead of 100 nF is a 10x cutoff error), assuming a value is a standard preferred one when the parts bin only stocks a different series, and -- most often -- never recomputing the cutoff after the substitution at all, so the actual error is simply unknown rather than small.

Does this calculator replace understanding preferred-value series like E12 and E24?

No, and it isn't trying to. Knowing that components come in E12/E24 steps rather than arbitrary values is still useful background. What this tool removes is redoing the arithmetic by hand every time: it solves for the exact component a target cutoff needs, snaps that to the nearest value in the series you'd actually buy, and reports the cutoff and signed error percent that snapped value really produces -- so the gap between "designed for" and "built with" is a number on the page instead of a guess.

Does this tool store or upload the values I enter?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser -- the components and target cutoff you enter, and the result it computes, never leave this page, and there is no account, upload, or server involved.

Open the RC / RL filter cutoff calculator and switch to "I have a target cutoff -- find a component" to try this.

rc-time-calculator/how-long-until-a-capa.text:
How long until a capacitor is fully charged?

Never, exactly — an RC charge only ever gets closer to the supply, not all the way there. What matters in practice is how close, and how long that takes. Put in your own R, C, and supply, and see. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

← RC charge and discharge time calculator · All free electronics tools

Your circuit's settling table

Default 100 nF, written as 0.0000001 F.

Time to a target percent

Not one of the rows above? Pick any percent below 100 and get the exact time for your own R and C.

Common questions

How long until a capacitor is fully charged?

There is no exact answer, because an RC charge never mathematically reaches 100% — it only gets closer and closer, forever. What people usually mean is one of a few conventions stated in time constants (τ = RC). On this page's defaults (10 kΩ, 100 nF, 5 V supply, so τ = 1 ms): 4τ reaches 98.17%, 5τ reaches 99.33%, and 10τ reaches 99.995%, indistinguishable from full for almost any purpose. Pick your own R, C, and supply above to see the real numbers for your circuit.

Why doesn't a charging capacitor ever reach exactly 100%?

Because the rate it charges at is proportional to how far it still has to go. The voltage follows V(t) = Vs(1 − e^−t/RC): every additional time constant closes 63.2% of whatever gap is left, not a fixed amount of voltage. Closing 63.2% of a gap can shrink that gap forever without ever making it zero, the same way repeatedly halving a distance never quite reaches the wall — it is arithmetic, not a limitation of any particular circuit.

Is 5 time constants really "fully charged"? How close is that?

5τ reaches 1 − e^−5 = 99.326% of the supply — a common convention, but a convention, not a law. On this page's own defaults that is 4.9663 V out of a 5 V supply, 3.37 mV short. Whether that is close enough depends entirely on what the circuit does next: 0.67% off is nothing for an indicator LED and can be a real error for a precision ADC reference.

How do I find the time for a different threshold, like 99.9%?

Use the target-percent tool above rather than reading the fixed table: it inverts the same equation, t = −RC × ln(1 − P/100), for any P you choose. On this page's defaults, 99.9% takes 6.9078 time constants — 6.9078 ms — noticeably longer than the 5τ convention for one more '9' of precision, which is the general shape of an exponential tail: each added 9 costs roughly one more time constant (ln 10 ≈ 2.303τ per decade).

Does this apply to discharging too, not just charging?

Yes, symmetrically. A discharging capacitor follows V(t) = V0 × e^−t/RC, closing 63.2% of the remaining voltage every time constant on the way down to zero instead of up to the supply — same τ = RC, same never-quite-zero asymptote, same 5τ/99.33% convention, just approaching from the other direction. The parent RC calculator's own discharge mode uses the identical formula this page's table is built from.

RC charge and discharge time calculator

Choose a real voltage threshold. Calculate the delay from R and C, or work backwards from a target time to a preferred part value. Nothing is uploaded.

Timing

Operation

For charge, this is the voltage reached from 0 V.

Not aiming for a specific voltage? How long until a capacitor is basically fully charged? — the 1τ–10τ settling table and why it never reaches 100%.

Voltage after a delay

The inverse question: you already have R, C, and a clock edge. What voltage is on the capacitor then?

Design a delay

Common questions

Why does τ = RC matter, and what is a “time constant”?

τ = RC is the time it takes an RC circuit to close about 63.2% of the gap to its final voltage — that 63.2% figure is 1 − 1/e, and it is where the “time constant” name comes from. This page's own defaults show it directly: R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF give τ = 1 ms, and the default threshold of 3.16 V is exactly 63.2% of the 5 V supply — charging to it takes 999.7 µs, essentially one full time constant.

What does “voltage after a delay” answer that the timing section doesn't?

It's the inverse question. Timing asks “how long until I reach this voltage?”; this asks “what voltage is on the capacitor after this much time?” Using this page's own defaults, after exactly 1 ms of charging (one time constant) the capacitor sits at 3.1606 V, 63.21% of the 5 V supply — the same 63.2% figure the first question describes, reached from the other direction.

Why does the design tool pick a slightly different part than the exact math?

Because resistors and capacitors are only sold in a fixed set of standard values (E24 for resistors, E12 for capacitors), not any number the algebra produces. Asking this page's own default 1 ms target time to solve for resistance (with the default 100 nF capacitor) calls for an exact 10003.28 Ω — but the nearest standard value happens to be 10 kΩ, which is itself an E24 value, so the snapped part still lands the delay at 999.7 µs, only 0.03% off target. A less convenient target time can snap by several percent instead.

Resistor Color Code & Ohm's Law Calculator

Decode a resistor's color bands into its resistance and tolerance, or solve Ohm's law (V, I, R, P) from any two known values. Everything runs in this page — nothing is uploaded.

← All free electronics tools

Resistor color code

LED series resistor calculator

Choose a resistor for one LED. The result includes resistor dissipation and a wattage recommendation with a 2× safety margin.

Enter all three values above.

Ohm's law & power solver

Fill in exactly two fields; the other two are computed (V = IR, P = VI).

Enter any two values above.

Common questions

What resistor does yellow-violet-red-gold decode to?

This calculator's own default bands — yellow (4), violet (7), red (×100), gold (±5%) — decode to 4.7 kΩ ±5%, one of the most common values in a beginner's kit. The first two bands give the significant digits (47), the third multiplies by 100, and the fourth is the tolerance band.

Why does the LED resistor calculator ask for exactly three values?

Because a series resistor's job is to burn off whatever voltage is left after the LED, at a set current — three knowns (supply voltage, LED forward voltage, target current) solve for the one unknown (resistance). Using the page's own placeholders — 5 V supply, a 2 V forward-voltage LED, 20 mA target — the required resistor is 150 Ω, dissipating 60 mW, for which this calculator recommends a 0.25 W part (it doubles the dissipation before picking a standard wattage, so the resistor runs at roughly half its rated power).

Why does the Ohm's law solver want exactly two fields, not four?

Voltage, current, resistance, and power are tied together by V = IR and P = VI, so any two of the four fix the other two — a third value would either be redundant or contradict the first two, which is why the solver rejects anything but exactly two filled fields. Enter, say, 5 V and 220 Ω and it solves the rest: 22.727 mA and 113.636 mW.

resistor-calculator/vs-reading-the-color.text:
This calculator vs. reading the resistor color code by eye

Reading bands by eye is fast and usually right -- until lighting, fading, or color vision turns one band into another. This tool doesn't change what the color code means; it removes the one step that eyesight and lighting can corrupt: matching a physical color to its name.

← Resistor color code & Ohm's law calculator · All free electronics tools

What each approach actually answers

Reading the bands by eye answers "what color am I looking at?" -- a perceptual question, not a knowledge one. Knowing the code perfectly (black-brown-red-orange-yellow-green-blue-violet-grey-white) doesn't help if warm indoor lighting has shifted a brown band toward red, if the resistor has faded sitting in a parts bin, or if you have red-green colorblindness and brown, red, orange, and green are hard to tell apart by name in the first place.

This calculator answers a narrower, more reliable question: "given these named colors, what resistance and tolerance do they decode to?" You still make the one judgment call the tool can't make for you -- which band is which -- but you make it by choosing from a list of named options rather than by perceiving and recalling a color correctly, and every lookup and multiplication after that point is exact.

Neither replaces the other. The color code itself doesn't change; what changes is whether the step most likely to go wrong is a color judgment or a menu selection.

Where reading by eye typically goes wrong

SituationWhat it does to a by-eye read
Warm or dim indoor lightingShifts perceived hue -- brown and red, or orange and yellow, become harder to tell apart.
A faded or dusty resistorDulls every band, so gold's shimmer can read as a worn yellow or orange, and silver as a dull grey.
Red-green colorblindnessCan make red, brown, orange, and green mutually hard to distinguish by name -- exactly the digit and multiplier bands most likely to be misread as each other.
A misread digit or multiplier bandChanges the decoded resistance by a factor of 10, 100, or more -- the resistor gives no other sign that the wrong color was read.
A misread tolerance bandSilently swaps a ±5% part for a ±10% or ±20% one, with no visible symptom until the circuit is built.

This calculator can't see the resistor either -- it can only compute correctly once you've told it which color each band is. What it removes is guessing or recalling that color from memory; you choose it from a labelled list instead.

Common questions

Isn't reading resistor colors easy once you know the code?

Under good lighting, on a fresh resistor, with normal color vision -- yes, it's quick. The failure cases are specific and common rather than rare: warm indoor lighting shifts brown toward red, a resistor that has sat in a dusty parts bin fades and dulls its bands, and red-green colorblindness (which affects a real share of readers, mostly men) makes red, brown, orange, and green hard to tell apart by name. None of that is a knowledge problem -- knowing the code perfectly doesn't help if the color in front of you isn't the color it looks like.

What mistakes does reading bands by eye typically cause?

The classic ones: red mistaken for brown or orange (a factor-of-10 error in a digit or the multiplier), gold's shimmer mistaken for a faded yellow or orange band, and silver confused with a dull grey. Each of these changes the decoded resistance by 10x, 100x, or more, or silently swaps a +/-5% part for a +/-10% one -- and the resistor gives no other clue that the wrong color was read.

Does this calculator replace learning the color code?

No, and it isn't trying to. Understanding what the bands mean is still useful for spotting a result that looks wrong. What this tool removes is the one step that lighting, fading, and color vision can all corrupt: matching a physical color to a name. You still pick the band; the tool just shows you the color names as a labelled list instead of asking you to recall or perceive them correctly, and it never mis-multiplies once a color is chosen.

Does this tool store or upload the colors I select?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser -- the bands you pick and the resistance it computes never leave this page, and there is no account, upload, or server involved.

voltage-divider-calculator/how-do-i-choo.text:
How do I choose resistor values for a loaded voltage divider?

Size the divider's own current well above what the load draws, and the output stays close to your target. Say how much stiffer you want it than the load and this page gives you R1/R2 — plus what the buyable pair actually delivers. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

← Voltage divider calculator · All free electronics tools

Size the divider

Enter the supply, the output you want, and the load it has to drive. The bleeder multiple sets how much bigger the divider's own current is than the load's — 10× is a common starting point.

Common questions

How do I choose resistor values for a voltage divider with a load?

Pick R1 and R2 so the current flowing through the divider itself is several times larger than the current the load draws — a common rule of thumb is 10 times. The bigger that ratio, the less the load's own current disturbs the split, so the output stays close to the unloaded value. The trade-off is power: a stiffer divider wastes more of it, all the time, whether the load is connected or not.

What is bleeder current?

The current that flows through R1 and R2 themselves, independent of whatever the load draws. It exists purely to hold the output steady against loading — the name comes from older bleeder resistors placed across a supply to drain it safely, and the term stuck for any divider current kept deliberately higher than the load needs.

Why not just pick a huge bleeder multiple and forget about droop entirely?

Because the quiescent power the divider burns scales directly with the bleeder current, and that current flows all the time, loaded or not — a stiffer divider is a hotter, more wasteful one, especially on a battery-powered design. It is a real trade-off, not a solved problem: pick the smallest multiple that gets the droop you can live with, and if no multiple gets there without excessive power, that load is telling you to use a proper regulator instead.

Is a resistive divider ever the right way to power something with a load?

Only for light, fairly constant loads where a percent or two of droop and some wasted power are acceptable — biasing a sensor, feeding a comparator reference, or a similar low-current job. For anything that draws meaningful or varying current, a resistive divider is a voltage reference, not a regulator, and a proper linear or switching regulator (or at least a unity-gain buffer) is the right tool.

Voltage Divider Calculator

What does R1/R2 actually give you at Vout — and how much does connecting a real load pull that down? Everything runs in this page — nothing is uploaded.

← All free electronics tools

Divider output

A real load in parallel with R2 pulls Vout down from the unloaded value — the higher R1/R2 are relative to the load, the worse the sag. Fill this in to see the real-world number, not just the textbook one. Know the load and want R1/R2 sized to resist it? See the divider-for-a-load calculator.

Design for a target output

Pick R1, say what Vout you want, and get the R2 you need — exact, and the nearest resistor you can actually buy.

Common questions

How much does a load pull down a divider's output?

It depends on how the load resistance compares with R2, since a load at Vout sits electrically in parallel with R2. With this page's own defaults — 12 V in through R1 = 10 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ — the unloaded output is 6.0000 V. Connect a 10 kΩ load and the effective R2 halves to 5 kΩ, so the output falls to 4.0000 V, a 33.33% drop. A load much larger than R2 barely moves the output; a load equal to R2 cuts it by a third, and a load smaller than R2 sags it further still.

Why does the target-output tool suggest a different R2 than the exact math gives?

Because real resistors only come in a fixed set of standard values — the E24 series this calculator snaps to — not any number the arithmetic happens to produce. Asking for 3.3 V out of a 12 V supply through a 10 kΩ R1, for example, calls for an exact R2 of 3793.10 Ω, a value nobody sells. The nearest E24 value is 3.9 kΩ, which the calculator recommends instead; wired up, it actually delivers 3.3669 V, about 2.03% high of the 3.3 V target, and the price of using a resistor you can actually buy.

Why shouldn't I use a plain resistive divider to power something?

Because, as the first question shows, its output voltage changes the moment real current is drawn — it is a voltage reference, not a regulator. It's a reasonable choice for feeding a high-impedance point such as an ADC input, which draws very little current; for a load that draws real current, use a proper linear or switching regulator instead. It also wastes power on its own: at the page's default 12 V, 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ, the divider dissipates 3.6 mW in R1 and 3.6 mW in R2 even before anything is connected to Vout.

vs-doing-the-math-by-hand.html.text:
← Free electronics calculators

These calculators vs. doing the math by hand

Every formula here -- Ohm's law, the LED resistor equation, a loaded voltage divider, 555 timer design, an RC/RL time constant -- can be worked by hand with a datasheet and a calculator app. This page names no specific product or company; it compares against that generic method, not a competing tool.

What each is for

Doing the math by hand gets the formula right as often as the person applying it does. Every equation these six tools use is published and ordinary: nothing here is beyond what a datasheet, a textbook, or a search already gives you, and a careful hand calculation reaches the same number the calculator does.

These calculators run the same formula, then take two steps a hand calculation usually leaves for later. Where a tool has a design mode — LED, voltage-divider, 555-timer, RC-filter, and RC-time — it snaps the computed value to the nearest standard E24 resistor or capacitor and shows the exact pair to buy, instead of leaving an odd value like 8,342 Ω to round and re-check by hand. The 555-timer calculator also flags a design a real chip cannot run: a duty cycle at or below 50%, an R1 that over-currents the discharge pin, or drift-prone resistor values. The voltage-divider calculator applies the loading correction a bare Vout = Vin × R2/(R1+R2) hand formula omits, which is why a real 1 kΩ load pulls a 12V/10k/10k divider well below the textbook 6V answer.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can I get the same number by working the formula out by hand?Yes — every formula here is a standard, published equation.
Does a hand calculation automatically round to a resistor or capacitor I can buy?Not on its own — that E24 rounding is a separate step these tools do for you.
Does a hand-calculated 555 design automatically run on a real chip?Not necessarily — this tool's 555 calculator flags an over-current or invalid duty cycle a formula alone would not catch.
Does the textbook voltage-divider formula account for a real load?No — this tool's loading correction does; a bare formula assumes nothing draws current.
Do I need an account or sign-up to use the calculator?No — same as a pocket calculator or a piece of paper.

Neither replaces reading a datasheet or measuring the circuit you actually built. A hand calculation and these tools reach the same formula's answer; the tools spend less time getting from that answer to a buyable part and a chip that can actually run the design.

These tools need no account and no sign-in: each is a static page, every calculation runs in your browser, and once a page has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Can I just work these formulas out by hand?

Yes. Ohm's law, the LED series-resistor equation, a loaded voltage divider, the 555 astable/monostable equations, an RC or RL time constant, and a resistor's color-code value are all standard formulas you can write down from a datasheet or a textbook and evaluate with any calculator app. Nothing about them requires a purpose-built tool to compute correctly once.

Where does a hand calculation usually stop short?

Two places. First, the raw answer is rarely a resistor or capacitor you can buy — a hand calculation gives you 8,342 ohms and leaves rounding it to a real E24 part, and re-checking the result still meets spec at that rounded value, as a separate step that is easy to skip under time pressure. Second, a 555 design that solves the formula can still be one a real chip cannot run — a duty cycle at or below 50% in the standard astable topology, an R1 low enough to over-current the discharge pin, or resistor values so large that leakage and drift dominate — and a hand calculation that only checks the formula has no reason to catch any of those on its own.

What do these calculators do that a hand calculation does not do for you?

Where a tool has a design mode — the LED, voltage-divider, 555-timer, RC-filter, and RC-time calculators — it runs the same formula you would write by hand, then snaps the result to the nearest standard E24 resistor or capacitor and shows the exact pair to buy, and the 555-timer calculator additionally flags a duty cycle at or below 50%, an over-current risk on the discharge pin, or drift-prone resistor values. The voltage-divider calculator also applies the loading correction a bare Vout = Vin × R2/(R1+R2) hand formula omits, which is why a real 1k load pulls a 12V/10k/10k divider well below the textbook 6V answer.

If I can already do this by hand, is there a reason to use the calculator instead?

Only if you want the E24 rounding and the chip-feasibility checks done for you, and want to avoid re-deriving the loading correction or the 555 feasibility rules from memory each time. If you would rather work the formula by hand and already know the E24 series and the 555's operating limits, a hand calculation is exactly as correct.

Is anything typed into these calculators uploaded anywhere?

No. Each calculator is a static page that runs entirely in your browser; nothing you type is uploaded anywhere, the same as working the formula on paper or in an offline calculator app.
